“The political agreement is there. We just need to work out the technicalities,” she said after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
The EU has been mulling introducing the ban for months – but has faced questions over how it could be enforced.
The push has gained traction as fears have risen over what Western officials describe as Moscow’s “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference in Europe .
Alongside that there are also discussions on limiting travel for Moscow’s diplomats and tightening criteria for tourist visas for Russians.
“One important element is to reduce the security risks inside our borders,” Kallas said.
European ⁠Union foreign ministers have ⁠a ⁠clear understanding ​that now is ⁠not the moment to ease ⁠pressure on ​Russia, ‌Kaja ‌Kallas, the bloc’s ‌foreign policy chief, told reporters on Monday.

Ukraine has passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, in a move expected to remove a major stumbling block to the country’s EU ambitions.
Hungary had been blocking the opening of so-called negotiation “clusters” – policy areas with which EU candidates must align their laws – accusing Kyiv of failing to protect the rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority.
Ukraine has long said it respected minority rights but nonetheless negotiated with Budapest over a possible law in a bid to accelerate its EU bid.
Kyiv’s parliament voted Monday to pass the legislation, which president Volodymyr Zelenskyy then signed into law, his office said.
“A Ukrainian law has been passed that ensures the rights of national minorities without compromising the status of the Ukrainian language,” the parliamentary press service said.
Russia ⁠carried ​out drone strikes on various targets ⁠in Ukraine on Monday, including on vessels ⁠carrying military cargo, ​Russia’s ‌defence ‌ministry said.

“For Germany and for Europe, such a decision is out of the question,” said Merz, referring to the US-Russia diesel deal.
“Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure and that is why we are maintaining our sanctions against Russia.”

Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks killed six people in two Ukrainian cities yesterday.
In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, a strike on a grocery store killed three people and injured 20 others, including two children, the regional governor, Oleh Syniehubov, said.
Footage released by the Kharkiv prosecutor’s office captured the moment of the strike, showing debris flying through the air and fires breaking out as car alarms sounded.

At least 150 Intermarche shops were targeted, along with almost 100 Cooperative U outlets, AFP reports. Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, with media reporting that hackers were “managing to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores.”
Reuters is carrying some further quotes from Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe , Gen Alexus Grynkewich , about how the alliance says it would deal with an attack on Nato territory. He told the audience at the Warsaw Security Forum:
If someone ​is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight. We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, ⁠proves utterly futile.
Should the adversary ​choose to press ‌the attack ​or commit his reserves, ​we will break the warfighting system engaged against us. This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force.
The US general is speaking just days after president Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel .
Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe , Gen Alexus Grynkewich has been outlining what he describes as the Nato “theory of victory”, in which he says Nato forces would block, then blunt, then break any aggressive move against the alliance.
While stressing that he did not see conflict as “inevitable”, he said at the Warsaw Security Forum it was a plan to “prepare us to execute our most sacred task – the defence of our people and our territory.”

If they truly want to hold elections in Kyiv, then the president of Russia, the commander-in-chief, will be ready to give an order not to launch strikes on Ukraine on election day, specifically on election day.

A government source told journalists last week that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations, which have shaken an unpopular government trying to reduce a ballooning budget deficit, was already “at least 30 million euros”.
Widespread disillusionment has seen young people protest over recent weeks against what they say is underfunding and neglect of the education system, with the demonstrations marred by often violent clashes that have injured hundreds.
Trying to appease the student’s demands, the government announced last week that about 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
But the Union of High School students described the initial announcements as “crumbs” and maintain their demand for an extra €10m (£8.4m) to be invested in the country’s lycees, where students – most between 15 and 18 – complete their high school education.

items.title: Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz - Al Jazeera
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Share Iran sets crosshairs on ‘US-UAE’ oil shuttle out of Strait of Hormuz on social media
Ships float anchored off the coast of Khasab in Oman’s Musandam Governorate, near the Strait of Hormuz, on October 2, 2026 [AFP]
Tehran, Iran – Iranian authorities have signalled they intend to disrupt an Arab-operated and United States-assisted shuttle system that has enabled more energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran.
With the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place and sanctions tightening, Tehran has said it will pursue military and diplomatic efforts to put pressure on Washington to submit to its demands regarding reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 What new measures is Iran taking to counter US economic pressure?
list 2 of 3 Saudi Arabia says East-West pipeline pumping 5.8 million bpd
list 3 of 3 Hormuz ship attacks surge: Are increased oil exports sustainable?
This strategic waterway, through which roughly a fifth of global oil and gas flowed before the war, has been largely closed to shipping following Iranian attacks since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
But the US Navy has reportedly opened up a route so Gulf states can export oil and other commodities amid an energy crisis.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei responded on Sunday night, saying the shuttle system is now an explicit target for Tehran.
Rezaei claimed that the US Central Command, with the assistance of the United Arab Emirates military, was using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers. He claimed Iran had been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks.
“You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.
This appeared to be a taunt aimed at US President Donald Trump, who has hailed energy exports at times reaching pre-war levels over recent weeks.
Rezaei appeared to give the impression that Iran wants to have lasting authority over Hormuz, and promised a harsh response if Iran’s energy and civilian infrastructure were attacked again.
His threats appeared aimed at Arab regional states, with a warning that digital infrastructure could be targeted. Rezaei threatened US-linked cables, data centres and artificial intelligence facilities in the UAE and around the Strait of Hormuz.
A woman rides her scooter past Iranian Zolfaghar missiles placed in front of a billboard of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei at Baharestan Square in downtown Tehran, Iran, September 28, 2026 [Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA] Rezaei also accused Saudi Arabia of helping the US move oil around Iran’s restrictions. But he did not threaten a direct attack against Riyadh – which is currently being targeted by Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis.
In early September, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) threatened tankers at ports and anchorages in Kuwait and Bahrain, citing US attacks on Iranian tankers . It accused both countries of complicity through hosting US armed forces.
Iran has claimed the US accepted some of Tehran’s seven conditions for the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war. But Tehran insists that a deal will only materialise when all its demands are met.
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, said this reflects Tehran’s apparent assessment that it is under no immediate pressure to reach an agreement with the US since its pressure in the Hormuz has a global impact.
“The question, however, is whether Tehran is overestimating its ability to sustain this pressure, given the growing economic costs of the confrontation for Iran itself,” Azizi wrote on X.
The system involves very large crude carriers (VLCCs) and smaller vessels coordinating with the US military to load crude oil at Arab ports and use southern corridors near the coast of Oman to exit the strait.
Vessels often switch off their transponders and travel at night to minimise the risk of being targeted by the Iranians. After ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, some of the shuttles come back to load more.
Multiple vessels were targeted overnight Sunday to Monday, including two outbound tankers and one in anchorage near Oman’s port city of Sohar, where ship-to-ship transfers are allegedly being conducted.
Other vessels were targeted by projectiles last week, indicating that attacks have extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz to target the shuttle system.
The IRGC has also increasingly driven a narrative that naval mines, believed to have been planted across the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war, pose a serious threat to vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without coordinating with Iran’s Persian Gulf Strait Authority.
The IRGC said three tankers suffered major damage over the weekend after being struck by mines. It also released footage of one ship ablaze that is said to have been struck by a mine, although the footage did not appear to show a mine going off.
The shuttle system has provided Arab national oil companies with a way out of Hormuz via the southern corridor near Oman.
Michelle Wiese Bockmann, a London-based senior maritime intelligence analyst at Windward, said this system has proven highly effective.
“Under international maritime law, which underpins 11 billion tonnes of seaborne trade annually, vessels have what’s called the right of transit passage,” Bockmann told Al Jazeera. “So, what Oman has done is allow vessels to go through under international maritime law, but they have had US military assistance.”
Tehran says shipping will be disrupted so long as the US continues its choking naval blockade against Iran, which has also stepped up its efforts to counter efforts by Arab states to export oil. At least 15 ships are believed to have been targeted in October so far, according to Winward.
“The more effective the route has become in facilitating the transport of oil and gas, the less leverage Iran has over Hormuz, and more attacks we are seeing on vessels that are using that southern corridor,” Bockmann said.
Windward’s data shows 31 ships transited the Strait of Hormuz daily in the final week of September. This was considerably lower than the 138 before the war.
Eighty-seven percent of the 45 ships targeted by Iran during the third quarter of 2026 were tankers.
Around 47 percent belonged to Gulf Arab energy companies’ national shipping fleets, Windward noted, and 93 percent of the strikes took place in the Strait of Hormuz. Most attacks targeted vessels transiting the southern corridor with their transponders turned off.
These attacks have contributed to a massive increase in freight costs. Freight represented 25-30 percent of Gulf crude’s cost, versus just 1 to 3 percent before the war, according to Windward. National oil companies have resorted to offering discounts of up to $35 per barrel below official selling prices.
The main reason for the rise is a shortage of tankers willing to make the dangerous crossing. Between 15 and 20 percent of very large crude carriers (VLCCs) are tied up with an inefficient logistics system that relies on shuttle transfers, complicated by escalating attacks and exposure at loading ports and anchorages.
“This is having cascading impacts for all vessel classes on freight and values across the world,” Bockmann said.

Microsoft will mainly use its Maia chips for AI inference
Microsoft said it will eventually have multiple gigawatts worth of its Maia AI chips.
The company intends to make Maia its primary architecture for running AI models.
The next-generation Maia 300 chip enters production in 2027.
Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.
Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.
Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .
The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.
For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."
Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.
Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.
"We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.

items.title: ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? - Al Jazeera

items.content:
Share ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil? on social media
Smoke billows from a fire at oil refinery, owned by Russian oil producer Gazprom Neft, in Moscow, Russia [File: Tatyana Makeyeva/Reuters]
US President Donald Trump has announced an immediate “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine, days after easing sanctions on Russian fuel to tackle soaring domestic and global fuel prices.
The energy truce, announced on Sunday, marks another shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy, as the Iran-US war and recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities disrupted global oil supplies and pushed up fuel prices. Trump has even asked Ukraine not to attack Russian oil facilities, as Moscow remains a major exporter of diesel.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Trump calls on Ukraine to replace Zelenskyy amid tensions over Russia deal
list 2 of 3 Hormuz attacks intensify as efforts to end war on Iran stall
list 3 of 3 Oval Office spat to public rebukes: A timeline of Trump-Zelenskyy ties
The spike in diesel prices in recent weeks has particularly put pressure on Trump’s Republican Party ahead of November’s midterm elections. Surveys show Americans hold the Trump administration responsible for the soaring fuel prices amid the unpopular US war on Iran.
“Attacks on refineries and energy facilities have taken capacity out of an already stretched global fuel market, pushing up costs for transport, agriculture and businesses, with the pain ultimately passed on to consumers,” Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera, referring to the mutual attacks on energy sites by Ukraine and Russia.
“A genuine ceasefire could help protect supplies and ease some of that pressure, particularly as winter approaches.”
However, she warned it was too early to call it a “diplomatic breakthrough”, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s statement that the energy truce came as a surprise to him.
Trump’s decisions have drawn criticism from US politicians and European allies, who warn that allowing Russian fuel back into global markets could provide Moscow with new revenue to finance its war in Ukraine. In March, the Trump administration gave a sanctions waiver to Russian seaborne oil.
So, why has Trump repeatedly changed his position on Russian energy, and what is behind his latest decisions?
On Sunday, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to immediately stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure.
“Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on Truth Social, without providing further details.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was not aware of the energy truce, saying the deal was “news to me” but welcomed the announcement nonetheless.
However, he said Russian drones continued targeting Ukrainian energy facilities, including a power plant in Kharkiv, after Trump’s statement.
“We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, ⁠⁠⁠⁠and we are waiting ⁠⁠⁠⁠to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take,” Zelenskyy said on Monday during a video address to a security conference in Warsaw.
“This ⁠⁠⁠⁠energy ceasefire, it can work, and it can become a major step towards ending ‌‌‌‌the war if the Americans truly step in now and make ‌‌‌‌sure ‌‌‌‌Russians respect it.”
(Al Jazeera) Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, arguing that energy revenues help fund Moscow’s war . Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukraine’s electricity and heating infrastructure throughout the four-year conflict.
Academic Alexey Muriaev has urged caution over Trump’s announcement, questioning whether an agreement has actually been reached, and if so, what it entails.
“Is it about suspending attacks on oil refineries? And if that’s the case, then the situation would be inadequate, because Ukraine’s oil refineries have already been taken out by Russia’s strikes beforehand,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in Defence and Strategic Studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
“So, in this sense, it would mean effectively Ukraine suspending unilateral action against Russia’s oil refinery facilities.”
Muriaev also linked the announcement to Trump’s diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting it may be a signal to Zelenskyy.
“Attacking Russian oil refinery capability would probably be interpreted by Washington as an attack on US economic interests,” he said, referring to the agreement on diesel exports through April 2027.
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine have continued to keep global oil markets under pressure.
On Monday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell to about $103.04 a barrel following Trump’s ceasefire announcement and Russian diesel deal, while US West Texas Intermediate crude traded at about $90.96.
However, prices remain elevated because of the US-Israel war on Iran, which began on February 28, and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies flow.
Recent attacks on Saudi oil installations and airports by Yemen’s Houthis and the fighting around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait have put further pressure on oil prices.
Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have compounded diesel shortages, affecting a fuel essential for the agriculture and trucking industries.
The crisis prompted the Group of Seven nations last week to agree to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves. The G7 decision came after pressure from Trump.
How has the Trump administration zig-zagged between punishing and embracing Russian energy?
Washington’s approach to Russian energy has shifted repeatedly since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Under President Joe Biden, the US banned Russian oil and energy imports in March 2022, seeking to cut off revenue used to finance Moscow’s war.
But Washington simultaneously supported a G7 price cap on Russian oil, designed to restrict Moscow’s earnings without removing too much supply from global markets.
Moreover, the Biden administration also accepted India’s continued purchases of Russian crude to prevent global prices from rising.
After returning to power last year, Trump initially intensified pressure on Moscow. In August 2025, his administration imposed additional tariffs on Indian goods over New Delhi’s purchases of Russian oil.
(Al Jazeera) Two months later, Washington sanctioned Russian energy giants Rosneft and Lukoil, accusing Moscow of failing to seriously pursue peace negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
However, Washington’s approach took a dramatic turn this year. On March 5, Washington issued a 30-day waiver allowing India to buy Russian oil stranded at sea, as disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid US attacks on Iran threatened global supplies.
A week later, the Trump administration expanded the exemption, allowing countries worldwide to buy sanctioned Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded onto tankers, with the waiver lasting until April 11.
In September, Trump urged Ukraine to stop attacking Russian refineries, blaming the strikes for global diesel shortages.
On October 9, he announced an agreement with Russian President Putin for Moscow to release more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, with another 1.5 million tonnes to follow.
Why has Trump changed his position on Russian oil frequently?
Trump’s shifting public position on Russian energy reflects ongoing, and often competing, political and economic pressures.
“Trump is caught between his geopolitical ambitions and the domestic political consequences of expensive energy,” Susannah Streeter of Wealth Club, told Al Jazeera.
She said Washington was trying to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine while simultaneously allowing Russian fuel sales that could generate additional revenue for the Kremlin.
“The shift may deliver a short-term political gain if supplies increase and prices ease, but it could come at a longer-term diplomatic cost,” she said, adding that the benefits appeared limited while the Middle East war continued.
US diesel prices reached a record $6.52 per gallon in September, placing Trump under pressure ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
However, according to academic Muriev, the US president’s public rhetoric should be distinguished from his administration’s actions.
“I don’t really see inconsistency in Trump’s approach because, apart from his public rhetoric, apart from his frequent media posting, there’s been a more steady approach on behalf of his administration,” he told Al Jazeera.
He pointed to discussions between Russian and American officials in August and September, suggesting that negotiations over the latest diesel agreement may have begun well before Trump’s announcement last Friday.
Muriev suggested the timing of the announcement could be politically motivated, allowing Trump to claim a victory on energy prices before the midterms.
Moreover, Moscow also has an interest in helping Trump retain political influence because his administration appears more willing to negotiate with Russia than former President Biden was. Trump has  been relatively more accepting of the Russian position on the Ukraine war and has even blamed Zelenskyy for failing to end the war.
“For Putin, it’s not just about scoring immediate economic benefit, but also achieving longer-term political and strategic goals,” Muriev said, referring to other issues such as Iran, cybersecurity, space cooperation and nuclear arms control.
The energy crisis has also created contrasting consequences for American businesses.
While higher oil prices can boost revenues for US energy producers, they increase operating costs for businesses dependent on fuel.
Susannah Streeter said cheaper diesel could provide relief to trucking companies, farmers and manufacturers, although the additional Russian supplies were unlikely to make a significant difference while disruptions in the Middle East continued.
She also warned that frequent changes to sanctions could create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment and supply-chain decisions.
“If sanctions are relaxed, reimposed or changed at short notice, companies face greater uncertainty over sourcing, compliance and the risk of being caught on the wrong side of a policy reversal,” she said.

items.title: Stock Market Warning Signal Seen Only 5 Times Since 1871 Points to Serious Downside Risk - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Stock Market Warning Signal Seen Only 5 Times Since 1871 Points to Serious Downside Risk  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Is now a good time to invest in stocks? Or is the stock market overheated, overpriced, and due for a big sell-off? The answer depends on your time horizon and overall financial goals. But some investors are worried about a widely respected valuation metric called the Shiller CAPE ratio. This metric keeps track of cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings for the S&P 500 index ( ^GSPC +0.05% ) .
The Shiller CAPE ratio uses stock market data going back to 1871. During the past 155 years, it has only peaked above 30 on five occasions. Several of those peaks happened right before big stock market downturns:
1999 -- right before the bursting of the dot-com bubble
As of this writing, the Shiller CAPE ratio had reached 41.8. That's its second-highest level of all time, higher than any time since 1999. Does this mean stocks are due for a crash ?
Not necessarily. No single valuation metric is 100% correct, and no way of looking at the stock market has a perfect track record of predicting the future. The S&P 500 moves up and down for all kinds of complex reasons.
The Shiller CAPE ratio is worth knowing about. But it doesn't mean you have to make big changes in your investment allocations. Let's see what the Shiller CAPE ratio could mean for your stock portfolio.
The Shiller CAPE ratio is well-respected by stock market analysts because it's a way to compare the S&P 500 index's valuation across long-term time frames. The CAPE ratio effectively "smooths out" the ups and downs of S&P 500 earnings due to changes in the business cycle, such as recessions, and adjusts company earnings per share for inflation.
However, there are a few reasons why the historical data-based approach of the CAPE ratio might not be the best way to predict future performance of the S&P 500 today. The CAPE ratio doesn't include stock buybacks. It also uses Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) earnings, and GAAP standards have changed a lot since 1871. Another big limitation of the CAPE ratio is that it looks at S&P 500 performance during the past 10 years -- but today's stock prices are forward-looking, based on expectations of future earnings.
Should you keep buying the S&P 500 with a high CAPE ratio?
Ever since July 2009, the CAPE ratio has been higher than its long-term average of 17. But rather than delivering weak returns (which a high CAPE ratio would seem to suggest), the stock market has delivered strong returns during that time.
For example, in the past 16 years since September 2010, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO +0.05% ) has delivered annualized returns of about 15%. That's much better than the S&P 500 long-term average of 10% annualized returns.
It's possible that the S&P 500 has reached a "new normal" regarding the CAPE ratio. Today's S&P 500 companies might just be more profitable and have stronger earnings potential compared to previous eras. The economy is a lot bigger than it was in 1871. 58% of Americans own stocks today, while in 1871, buying stocks was more of a pastime for only the richest people.
Is the Shiller CAPE ratio irrelevant or outdated? No. It can be a good tool, and it's worth watching. But don't assume that this one imperfect valuation method is 100% correct at predicting the future.

items.content:
This has been a year highlighted by a changing of the guard. Longtime CEOs Warren Buffett and Tim Cook handed over the keys to their respective successors, and President Donald Trump's Fed chair nominee, Kevin Warsh, became only the 17th head of the central bank on May 22.
Despite these changes, Wall Street's preeminent stock indexes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.50% ) , S&P 500 ( ^GSPC +0.04% ) , and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.19% ) have been unstoppable. The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out and otherworldly growth prospects accompanying this game-changing innovation have lifted the broader market to new heights.
This won't be a one-and-done rate-hiking cycle. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
But sustaining this AI-driven bull market could be easier said than done. Last week, Fed Chair Warsh and his Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) colleagues fired an unmistakable warning shot at the second-priciest stock market in history. The only question is: How many investors are paying attention?
The Federal Reserve's rate-hiking cycle is ramping up
On Sept. 16, Warsh and 11 other voting members of the FOMC unanimously raised the federal funds target rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%. It's just the fourth time this century that the central bank has kicked off a rate-hiking cycle .
Warsh and the FOMC have been compelled to act because of persistently elevated inflation. August marked the 66th consecutive month in which the annualized inflation rate topped the FOMC's long-term 2% target.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," https://t.co/htRQqyQHtr
While rising prices are perfectly normal in an expanding economy, inflation has soared in 2026 due to Trumpflation (inflation that's specifically driven by President Trump's policies). Donald Trump's tariffs are increasing domestic manufacturing costs, while the Iran war has led to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The largest energy supply disruption in modern history has sent fuel prices soaring.
The newly released Federal Reserve meeting minutes (effectively a summary of what policymakers discussed behind closed doors on Sept. 15-16) point to tariffs, the Iran war, and the AI infrastructure build-out as key sources of inflation.
More importantly, the Fed meeting minutes charted a path forward for interest rates. Contained in the Fed minutes was this statement:
With regard to the outlook for monetary policy beyond this current meeting, most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end. While this statement doesn't tell us whether the FOMC would raise interest rates at the October or December meeting, it makes it crystal clear that additional rate hikes are expected in the not-too-distant future. That's terrible news for a historically expensive stock market.

A truly jaw-dropping amount of capital is being spent on the AI data center build-out , part of which has been financed with debt. If lending costs rise, as the FOMC's September meeting minutes imply, it could slow this expansion and adversely impact lofty growth expectations.
In June, the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings Ratio came within a stone's throw of surpassing the priciest valuation multiple in 156 years , achieved just before the dot-com bubble burst. This is a stock market with little to no margin for error. If the Fed's rate-hiking cycle ramps up, maintaining this aggressive AI build-out without any "hiccups" would likely prove impossible.

India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
India’s consumer price inflation increased to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August.
India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, higher than its medium-term target of 4%.
Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival.
India's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August , adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.
The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.
India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release.
Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023 , joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.
India is among the countries most  vulnerable to the supply disruptions  caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the  Strait of Hormuz .
Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.
India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%.
The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.
Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino , with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs.
The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.
HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

Balkan temperatures swing as heavy rain heads for Greece
Clear skies bring warm days and cold nights to Montenegro, while a low-pressure system moves towards Aegean Sea
Temperatures fluctuated dramatically in the Balkans last week, with unusually large differences between daytime highs and overnight lows – known as the diurnal range.
An area of high pressure over the region brought prolonged sunshine during the day, while clear skies at night allowed temperatures to drop rapidly as heat escaped into the atmosphere without cloud cover to slow the cooling.
In Kosanica, Montenegro , the average maximum temperature in October is 15C (59F), while the average minimum is 4C. However, on 4 and 5 October the difference between daytime highs and overnight lows reached 30C, more than double the October average.
Elsewhere in Europe , high pressure will build across the north and west over the coming week, pushing an area of low pressure southwards towards the Mediterranean. The low-pressure system will deepen as it crosses the Adriatic and Ionian seas before moving eastwards into the Aegean Sea by the middle of the week.
Spells of heavy rain and strong winds are expected to sweep across Greece as a result. Forecast models suggest widespread rainfall of 50-150mm, with the highest totals expected around the island of Skiathos.
Towards the end of the week, the system will continue eastwards, bringing showers to parts of Crete, which was hit by severe flooding a week earlier. Those storms swept some cars and trees into the sea.
People cross a bridge over a swollen river as Hurricane Simon approaches Mexico’s Pacific coast in Costalegre, Jalisco state. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, a category 4 storm, is moving close to Mexico’s Pacific coast, near the state of Jalisco. It is the latest of 21 named storms in the Pacific this season, 11 of which have reached hurricane strength.
At the time of writing, Simon has a central pressure of 933mb and maximum sustained winds of nearly 150mph (241km/h). However, the hurricane is expected to weaken rapidly if its core moves onshore, cutting it off from the warm ocean waters that fuel it.
Heavy rainfall is affecting south-western Mexico, where totals could reach 300-400mm across a wide area, rising to 400-500mm in the wettest locations.

Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.
Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.
The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.
Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.
Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.
Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China .
On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.
Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.
“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.
Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.
The new all-electric ID Tiguan. Photograph: Volkswagen AG Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”
Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.
Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.
The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.
On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

Microsoft reveals Maia 300 AI chip as it works to reduce dependence on Nvidia, AMD
Microsoft ( MSFT ) has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia ( NVDA ) and AMD ( AMD ).
Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year.
The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services."
The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200.
Tokens are a basic unit of measurement in AI systems that can represent parts of words, images, and videos.
The more tokens per megawatt, the more efficient an AI rack.
Microsoft's Maia 300 processor. (Image: Microsoft) · Microsoft The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.
Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon ( AMZN ), Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), and Meta ( META ), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.
Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.
That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.
On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.
That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.

by Todd Bishop on Oct 12, 2026 at 6:22 am October 12, 2026 at 6:24 am
A prototype of Microsoft’s Azure Maia 300 chip, which the company plans to begin deploying at scale in 2027. (Microsoft Photo)
Microsoft plans to run most of its AI services on chips it designs itself, a shift that could save the company billions of dollars and reduce its dependence on industry juggernaut Nvidia.
The company on Monday unveiled Maia 300, the third generation of its custom AI chip, saying it will begin large-scale deployments in 2027. In a blog post , Azure chief Scott Guthrie said Maia will become “the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services.”
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called it “our biggest bet yet on our own silicon” in a post on X .
Maia 300 will produce 40% more AI output for the same amount of power as leading GPU-based systems, which Nvidia dominates, according to the company.
A full rack of the new chips will produce up to seven times as much AI output as the current generation, the company says. They’re designed for the kinds of tasks that are growing fastest, such as AI agents that work through multistep jobs and models that handle long documents or conversations.
The Redmond company designs the chips and relies on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) to make them, rather than buying finished chips from Nvidia. More-efficient chips also let Microsoft run AI services using less electricity, at a time when power supply has become one of the biggest constraints on AI expansion.
Microsoft and Nvidia remain big partners. Nadella and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang shared the stage last week to launch Windows PCs built on Nvidia chips. Nvidia also remains a key supplier for Microsoft’s data centers, and Nadella said on the company’s July earnings call that Microsoft will be among the first cloud providers to deploy next-generation systems based on Nvidia’s Vera Rubin and AMD’s Helios.
Microsoft’s move is part of a larger trend among tech giants to design their own AI chips. Google has started selling its Tensor Processing Units directly to some customers, and Amazon has won over AI companies including Anthropic with its Trainium chips. Meta has rolled out its own AI chips , and OpenAI unveiled its first custom chip , built with Broadcom, in June.
Microsoft has been playing catch-up. Unlike Google’s and Amazon’s chips, Maia isn’t available for outside customers to rent. Microsoft’s first Maia chip, announced in 2023 , was followed by a second-generation Maia 200 this January after delays. As of this summer, Maia 200 was running in just two U.S. data centers, The Information reported in August .
Maia 200, the current generation, already powers Microsoft 365 Copilot and runs models from OpenAI as well as Microsoft’s own. It’s now being deployed across the U.S., Europe and Australia, according to Microsoft. GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry are set to move onto it by the end of the year.
The shift will take time. Evercore ISI analysts estimate that Maia will account for about 10% of Microsoft’s spending on AI chips by early 2027, CNBC reported .
Microsoft says it will share more details next month at its Ignite conference in San Francisco.

Tom Warren is a senior correspondent and author of Notepad , who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.

Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.
Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie , executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.”

“Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.”

Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

Microsoft challenges Nvidia with new Maia 300 AI chip promising 40% greater efficienc
Microsoft challenges Nvidia with new Maia 300 AI chip promising 40% greater efficiency
Microsoft says its new in-house AI accelerator can generate 40% more tokens using the same power as competing GPU-based systems; deployment is set to begin in 2027, with the chip expected to become a central platform for the company's AI services
Microsoft on Monday unveiled Maia 300, a powerful new artificial intelligence chip developed in-house, along with a complete computing system designed to support it, as the technology giant steps up efforts to reduce its dependence on Nvidia and secure greater control over the infrastructure powering its AI services.
The company says the new chip and the system built around it can deliver 40% more AI output at the same level of electricity consumption as competing systems based on graphics processing units, or GPUs. Microsoft plans to begin deploying Maia 300 in 2027, when it is expected to become a central platform for running AI models across its products.
The announcement marks another step in the intensifying competition among technology giants to develop their own AI processors rather than rely heavily on Nvidia, whose chips continue to dominate the market for training advanced AI models.
Maia 300 is a specialized data center processor known as an AI accelerator. It was designed by Microsoft to run AI workloads in the massive data centers supporting its Azure cloud platform, with an emphasis on processing information quickly while using as little electricity as possible.
Microsoft is following a path already taken by Google, which developed its own Tensor Processing Units, or TPUs, and Amazon, which created its Trainium chips. All three companies are seeking to gain greater control over the hardware powering their growing AI operations.
For Microsoft, developing its own processors is also a way to prepare for surging global demand for AI computing power, reduce supply chain bottlenecks and secure a reliable supply of chips without depending entirely on external suppliers.
One of the main reasons behind Maia 300 is the rapid rise of AI agents, systems capable of carrying out complex tasks involving multiple steps rather than simply answering individual questions.
These agents require computing infrastructure capable of handling enormous amounts of information, responding quickly and operating efficiently over extended periods. Microsoft says Maia 300 was designed specifically for these increasingly demanding workloads.
From right: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. The companies remain close partners even as Microsoft works to reduce its dependence on Nvidia's chips
Unlike chips primarily used to train AI models, Maia 300 focuses on a process known as inference. This is the stage at which an already trained model processes a user's request and generates a response.
Training involves teaching a model to recognize patterns and develop capabilities using vast amounts of data. Inference is what happens afterward, when that model is put to work answering questions, analyzing information or completing tasks.
Nvidia's processors still dominate the training market, but Microsoft is positioning Maia 300 as a more efficient alternative for inference, particularly as AI agents become more capable and their computing requirements grow.
According to Microsoft, the new accelerator and its supporting system can produce 40% more tokens at the same power consumption as competing GPU-based platforms. Tokens are the basic units of text that AI models process and generate, making token throughput a key measure of performance for AI services.
Another major focus of Maia 300 is reducing the time needed to move data between the different components of an AI computing system.
In large AI models, information must constantly travel between memory and processors, as well as between multiple accelerators working together. These transfers can create bottlenecks that limit performance even when the processors themselves are extremely powerful.
Microsoft says Maia 300 addresses this problem with an architecture designed to speed up data movement and improve efficiency across the entire system.
The chip provides memory bandwidth of 18 terabytes per second, allowing it to feed large volumes of information to AI models at high speed and support workloads that require substantial memory capacity.
The company says these capabilities will be particularly important for the next generation of AI agents, which will increasingly need to analyze extensive information, maintain context across long interactions and complete complex, multistep assignments.
Maia 300 is not Microsoft's first attempt to develop its own AI hardware. The company already operates an earlier system, Maia 200, which supports its Copilot AI assistant and the team developing its next generation of AI models.
Microsoft plans to expand the earlier system's use to additional services by the end of 2026, before beginning deployment of Maia 300 in 2027.
The transition reflects a broader shift in the AI industry. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in everyday software and AI agents take on more demanding tasks, the cost of running models is becoming increasingly important alongside the computing power required to train them.
For Microsoft, the potential benefits extend beyond performance. Developing its own chips could reduce reliance on Nvidia, ease pressure on hardware supply chains and give the company more control over the costs and availability of computing resources.
The two companies remain major partners, with Nvidia's technology playing an important role in Microsoft's AI infrastructure. But Maia 300 highlights Microsoft's determination to build an increasingly independent hardware ecosystem.
Whether the new chip can meaningfully alter the balance of power in the AI semiconductor market will depend on how it performs once deployment begins in 2027.

Record Profits at Samsung & TSMC Say the AI Trade Is Intact
Despite a questionable macro economy and soaring energy prices, equity markets have been buoyed by the massive, unprecedented artificial intelligence buildout. Just how impactful has the AI revolution been for the U.S. economy and stock market?
The massive wave of CAPEX spending on data centers, graphics processing units (GPUs), and energy has accounted for more than a quarter of total U.S. GDP growth, and now dwarfs every other major American infrastructure boom, including the Interstate Highway System, the Apollo space program, and the 19th-century railroad expansion. In other words, Wall Street's big question is: "How sustainable is AI spending?" The answer matters not only to the AI industry, but also for the U.S. economy and stock market as a whole.
Below are three clues that AI spending is sustainable for the foreseeable future, including:
Samsung Electronics is the world's largest memory manufacturer. AI data centers have driven insatiable demand for memory over the past few years. Last night, Samsung's earnings gave investors clues about AI spending. Samsung reported the most profitable quarter ever by any company ($80.2 billion). Samsung's main customers include Qualcomm , Alphabet, Tesla , Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon .
Memory makers aren't the only ones showing that AI growth remains scorching-hot. Taiwan Semiconductor , the world's largest manufacturer of AI chips, reported record Q3 revenue of $46.7 billion, up 50% year over year. TSM is a critical AI company to watch because it produces over 60% of all global contract chips and over 90% of advanced chips. NVIDIA , AMD, QCOM, Intel , Apple and Broadcom are all TSM customers.
Earlier this week, SpaceX announced it will raise $40 billion in debt to buy NVIDIA chips as it scales its AI compute. Although investors often frown upon debt offerings, SpaceX's compute economics are mind-boggling. For every dollar SpaceX spends bringing on AI compute, it's payback period is well under one year, thanks to lucrative deals with Google and Anthropic. In other words, SpaceX is proving that n AI compute investing not only makes sense, but the economics are also extremely attractive.
The sustainability question about the AI infrastructure buildout has been answered. Recent news from Samsung, TSMC, and SpaceX suggests record CAPEX spending will continue.

items.title: Immigration agents search Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
items.summary: Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
items.content:
US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC, area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.
The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said, but no further details were given.
Omar was born in Somalia and came to the US aged 12 after four years in a Kenyan refugee camp. First elected to Congress in 2018, she is running for reelection next month, and is an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump.
The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.
A statement from Rep. Omar's communications director Jacklyn Rogers called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies".
"The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies," it said.
A BBC crew saw several agents at the home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which has said the representative is being investigated over immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.
The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear, but it is not the first time her immigration records have been scrutinised by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar. Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar, a Democrat, denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email, an archive of which has been seen by the BBC.
She has been targeted by Trump with the president previously suggesting that she "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession."
The president also spoke unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."
Republicans celebrated the search. "Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota Representative Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"
Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.
She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote. The timing of Monday's raid â 22 days to the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power for the next two years â is likely to raise concerns from Democrats.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.

items.title: The Iran war didn't make your heating bill this high. Blue-state energy policy did - Fox News
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.?oc=5" targ
items.content:
Fox News senior White House correspondent Peter Doocy has the latest on the world's energy crisis and the G7 nations' big announcement on 'Special Report.'
Heating season is here, and the Iran war is getting the blame for higher energy prices . The war explains the timing. It doesn't explain the vulnerability.
America produces enormous amounts of oil and gas. Why do prices jump when the Persian Gulf flares? Because oil trades on a world market. A crisis anywhere moves prices everywhere.
But the real problem is policies at the state level that have kept us from truly unleashing the bounty of our domestic energy supply.
CHEVRON CEO WARNS IRAN CONFLICT HAS CREATED 'VERY REAL' THREAT TO GLOBAL OIL SUPPLIES AS GAS PRICES CLIMB
It’s been well documented that we have a refinery shortage. The country has 130 operable refineries, down from 301 in 1982, and no major new refinery has been built in the U.S. since 1976. Here in the Northeast, when we lost the Philadelphia Energy Solutions plant, we lost about 335,000 barrels a day.
A part of the Trans Alaska Pipeline System is seen on Sept. 17, 2019, in Fairbanks, Alaska. The 800-mile-long pipeline carries oil from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
In my home state of New York , like so many other states, we also have a self-imposed supply problem. Natural gas moves through pipelines, and New York has blocked those pipelines. Pennsylvania, right next door, sits on some of the richest gas fields in the country. The Constitution Pipeline, if constructed, would carry that natural gas 124 miles, with 99 miles of new right-of-way in New York.
AMERICAN BUSINESSES AREN’T ALLOWED TO BUILD. IT’S TIME CONGRESS HELPED THEM
The fight to build this much-needed pipeline is now 10 years old. In April 2016, the state denied the water permit. Courts upheld it. The company tried again in 2025, then withdrew in November after three notices that its application was incomplete.
And the problem runs deeper than one pipeline. Ill-conceived climate laws set sweeping emissions targets, and the plan to reach them is thin if not unattainable. Take New York City's Local Law 97. It fines large buildings that exceed emissions limits, and the limits tighten sharply in 2030. Owners must pay for costly retrofits or pay penalties. Either way, the bill lands on tenants, co-op owners and small businesses.
THE REAL REASON YOUR ELECTRIC BILL IS SOARING THIS SUMMER WILL SURPRISE YOU
Democrats in too many state capitals seem determined to choke off other reliable and cost-effective energy sources. Nuclear reactors and coal plants have closed down, both of which supply much-needed energy to citizens, especially low-income families.
Meanwhile, the utility bills keep climbing , filling your gas tank becomes more painful, and truckers and shippers face punishing prices for diesel, which, of course, trickles down to raise the cost of everything from lumber to lunch meat.
SENATORS PRESS PRESIDENT TRUMP TO RELEASE HOME HEATING OIL RESERVES AMID SOARING PRICES
I’ve spent over 20 years in the energy and utility industry. Energy is not abstract. It is pipe, wire, steel and supply. Limit supply while demand holds, and prices rise. That is arithmetic, not ideology.
And winter makes it more brutal. On the coldest days, when pipes run full, utilities scramble for alternatives and alternatives cost more. Families on fixed incomes can't opt out. They lower the thermostat and pull on another sweater.
TRUMP ADMIN MOVES TO GUT BIDEN'S SIGNATURE ENVIRONMENTAL RULES
Here is what should bother everyone, whatever their politics. A state that won't produce or import its own fuel doesn't become independent. It becomes a customer. It bids against the world for supply and accepts whatever price is asked, including prices set by wars it can't influence.
The fight to build this much-needed pipeline is now 10 years old. In April 2016, the state denied the water permit. Courts upheld it. The company tried again in 2025, then withdrew in November after three notices that its application was incomplete.
What's the solution? Approve pipeline projects with capacity that bring in domestic gas. Keep reliable power plants running until real replacements are built and tested. Approve the construction of new refineries. Be honest about what climate mandates cost and phase them in at a pace working families can afford. Judge success by lower bills and steady supply, not ribbon-cuttings.
And most importantly: Vote for candidates this November who are dedicated to American energy independence , supporting sensible and robust expansion of both production and refinement of our own bountiful energy supply.
Dave Bovee spent 20 years in the energy and utility industry. His book, "The Four G Revolution: The Fight to Save God, Gas, Guns, and Glory," was published by RealClear Publishing on October 6.
